title: Shipyard: Tenant sandboxing and throttled vGPU reservations for steady throughput guarantees
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Enable a declarative tenant sandboxing mechanism (Shipyard) that offers per-tenant soft vGPU reservations with throttled burst behavior to deliver predictable throughput SLAs. This ticket covers control-plane APIs, scheduler hooks, node-level enforcement, and an autoscaling policy that respects tenant contracts while mitigating noisy neighbors. Non-goal: full hard-guarantee physical GPU pinning or replacing cgroup-level resource management implemented by infra agents.
background: Customers buying Dedicated capacity need predictable per-tenant throughput under mixed workloads and noisy bursts. Current allocator provides best-effort fairness which can lead to tail latency spikes and SLA violations when noisy workloads (large batch decoding or speculative pipelines) appear. We need a pragmatic approach that: 1) isolates noisy tenants; 2) enforces per-tenant steady-state quotas; 3) allows controlled bursts subject to short-term admission; 4) integrates with autoscaler so capacity grows before SLA breach.
proposal_summary: Introduce 'Shipyard' tenant sandboxing: a control-plane contract object declaring steady_qps and burst_credits. The scheduler assigns vGPU reservations mapped to a tenant's steady footprint. Node agent enforces token-bucket cgroups for bandwidth/compute tokens and observes KV-cache influence. Autoscaler reacts to sustained queue depth and credit exhaustion to scale the tenant's dedicated lane. Implement graceful degradation by redirecting excess requests to cheaper model variants or slower pods and emit telemetry for rollback/alerting.
tradeoffs_and_risks: Soft reservations preserve utilization but allow transient contention — risk of SLA miss if autoscaling is slow
Token-bucket enforcement at process level requires kernel tuning and cross-GPU accounting — complexity on multi-GPU nodes
Admission control + redirection increases tail latency for some requests; customer-facing SLAs must document fallback behavior
Increased control-plane state per-tenant may add pressure to scheduler; we will shard Shipyard state and cache on nodes
implementation_plan: Control-plane API: ShipyardContract CRD-like object (steady_qps, burst_tokens, recovery_window, fallback_policy)
Scheduler hooks: reservation matcher that prefers colocated vGPU slots and respects topology-affinity; preemption policy for overloaded nodes
Node agent: token-bucket enforcement integrated with existing cgroup manager and nvml/metrics for per-process GPU time accounting
Autoscaler: new trend detector that triggers scale-up on sustained token exhaustion and queue growth (configurable lookback)
Fallbacks: implement model-variant routing rules (e.g., fp16->int8 or smaller context length) to preserve request completion during resource pressure
E2E tests: microbench harness simulating noisy neighbor (large decode), steady background traffic, and burst scenarios
Phased rollout: feature flag -> internal tenants -> opt-in customers -> default on for reserved contracts
acceptance_criteria: ShipyardContract objects can be created/updated via API and stored in control-plane DB
Node agents enforce token-bucket limits such that steady throughput remains within 5% of requested steady_qps under injected noisy workload
Autoscaler triggers scale-up within configured time window on sustained token exhaustion in at least 95% of test runs
Fallback routing successfully redirects >=90% of overflow requests to a fallback variant without throwing 5xx errors
Dashboard surfaces per-tenant tokens, exhaustion events, and autoscale actions; alerts fire when exhaustion persists > configured threshold
testing_notes: Create synthetic harness in bench/shipyard that runs multi-tenant interference profiles (image/seq2seq/batch-decoder)
Use chaos monkey to kill nodes to validate graceful reallocation and fallback behavior
Compare throughput with and without KV-cache warm state to ensure cache effects don't mask isolation regressions
rollout_plan: Stage 1 (internal): enable for infra/eval tenants for 2 weeks; collect metrics
Stage 2 (opt-in): invite 3 pilot customers with low-risk workloads; run per-customer smoke tests
Stage 3 (default-on for reserved): enable for new Dedicated contracts with clear documentation and opt-out clause
Fallback: automatic disable if token-exhaustion alert rate > 10% and SRE escalation not acknowledged within 1 hour

open_questions: What is appropriate default for burst_tokens and recovery_window for small (P2) vs enterprise (P0) tenants?
Should fallback policies be configurable per-route or per-tenant? (current proposal defaults per-tenant with per-route overrides)
Do we need hardware-level telemetry (nvml kernel traces) enabled for pilot tenants to diagnose subtle interference?
